claims.claim: Plutarch, Life of Solon 13, 14, 15, 18, 25; Life of Themistocles 22; Life of Alcibiades 13 are quoted verbatim from Plutarch's Lives vol. 1, tr. Aubrey Stewart and George Long (1880), Gutenberg #14033. Chapter numbers are the Roman numerals printed in the file.

Aristotle, The Athenian Constitution 12 (Solon's poems), 20–22, 42–43 are verbatim from F. G. Kenyon's translation (1891; Kenyon d. 1952), Gutenberg #26095; part numbers as printed ('Part 20' etc.). Part 43 is quoted only to its second paragraph.

Thucydides II.60 (opening of Pericles' last speech), II.65, III.36–50 are verbatim from Richard Crawley's translation (1874; d. 1893), Gutenberg #7142. Cuts marked '…': in Cleon's speech (III.39, Mytilene's offence) and in Diodotus' (III.43, on suspicion of speakers). III.50 ends at 'rather more than a thousand.'

Plato, Republic VIII.557a–558c, 561c–e, 562a–564a, 565c–566d, 569b–c and VI.488a–489c are verbatim from Jowett, Gutenberg #1497. Stephanus numbers are assigned by us from the standard text (Jowett's Gutenberg text has none).

Aristotle, Politics III.11 (whole chapter) and IV.11 (first five paragraphs, to 'form either a democracy or an oligarchy') are verbatim from the Gutenberg #6762 text. The file header names the translator as William Ellis (1776), not Jowett as the spec and plan say. Bracketed Bekker page numbers ([1282a], [1295b], [1296a], [1296b]) were removed; no other change.
Ellis's text of Politics III.11 reads 'Socrates, and some other legislators' where the Greek (1281b32) has Solon; the commentary says so.
claims.source: Aristotle, Politics 1281b32 (Greek text, e.g. Ross OCT)

claims.claim: Lord Acton, 'The History of Freedom in Antiquity' (address at Bridgnorth, 26 February 1877), in The History of Freedom and Other Essays (1907), Gutenberg #31278: three passages verbatim (Solon; Athens' failure; Christ and Caesar). Acton d. 1902.
claims.source: .cache/texts/31278.txt; footnote 2 of the essay gives place and date

claims.claim: The Mayflower Compact text is verbatim from the Avalon Project page (Yale), fetched as url/democracy-mayflower.txt; signed at Cape Cod, 11 November 1620 (Old Style), by 41 men.

Tocqueville quotation ('Religion in America takes no direct part in the government of society, but it must nevertheless be regarded as the foremost of the political institutions of that country') is verbatim from Reeve's translation, Gutenberg #815 (Democracy in America I.ii.9). Reeve d. 1895.

Scripture from WEB via web.py: Leviticus 25:8–17; Proverbs 29:2, 4, 12, 14, 18; Exodus 23:1–8; Deuteronomy 1:9–18; quoted verses Isaiah 1:17, Leviticus 25:23, 44–46, Exodus 21:2, Genesis 1:27, Galatians 3:28, Mark 12:17, Acts 5:29, John 8:32, Romans 13:1, Deuteronomy 17:20.

Solon archon 594 BC (traditional date); Peisistratus tyrant from 561 BC; Hipparchus killed 514; Hippias expelled 510; Cleisthenes' reforms 508/7; first ostracism 487; Marathon 490; Salamis 480; Ephialtes 462/1; citizenship law 451/0; last ostracism c. 417 (Hyperbolus); Mytilene 427; Arginusae 406; Thirty 404–403; Socrates 399; Macedon ends democracy 322.
claims.source: Athenian Constitution 14–26, 35–41; Thucydides; Xenophon, Hellenica I.7, II.3–4; P. J. Rhodes, Commentary (1981); M. H. Hansen (1991)

claims.claim: Draco's laws c. 621 BC; Kylon's attempt c. 632 BC.
claims.source: Athenian Constitution 4; Thucydides I.126; standard chronology

claims.claim: About 30,000 adult male citizens in the 300s BC, perhaps twice that in 431 BC; total population of Attica perhaps 250,000 or more.
claims.source: M. H. Hansen, The Athenian Democracy in the Age of Demosthenes (1991); estimates vary widely

claims.claim: Assembly met about 40 times a year on the Pnyx; quorum of 6,000 for some business; pay for attendance from c. 400 BC; jurors' pay introduced by Pericles in the 450s; 6,000 jurors enrolled yearly; panels of 201, 501 or more; kleroterion fragments in the Agora Museum.
Ostracism required at least 6,000 votes cast (one ancient account; another says 6,000 against one man).
More than 10,000 ostraka found, many in the Kerameikos excavations of the 1960s; 190 ostraka against Themistocles in a few hands found by Oscar Broneer on the north slope of the Acropolis (1937).
Moses Finley argued that the end of debt-bondage for citizens and the growth of chattel slavery went together.
claims.source: M. I. Finley, Economy and Society in Ancient Greece (1981), 'Between slavery and freedom' and 'Was Greek civilisation based on slave labour?'

claims.claim: Thorkild Jacobsen, 'Primitive Democracy in Ancient Mesopotamia', JNES 2 (1943).
Solon's Eunomia poem is fr. 4 West, quoted by Demosthenes 19.254–255; the Dark Earth poem is fr. 36 West, quoted in Athenian Constitution 12. Our summary of fr. 4 is in our own words.
claims.source: M. L. West, Iambi et Elegi Graeci II (1992)

claims.claim: Pericles' mother Agariste was a niece of Cleisthenes; Pericles elected general every year 443–429; called 'the Olympian' by comic poets; never increased his inherited estate by a drachma.
Pericles calls the empire a tyranny (II.63).
Plato's Gorgias 515c–516d: Socrates says Pericles made the Athenians idle, cowardly, talkative and greedy by introducing pay.
Aristotle's school says Cleon was the first to shout and abuse from the speaker's platform.
Aristophanes' Knights (424 BC) portrays Cleon as a fawning slave of Demos; Clouds (423 BC) mocks Socrates; Ecclesiazusae c. 391 BC.
Some editors think the 'more than a thousand' executed after Mytilene (III.50) is a corruption of a smaller number.
claims.source: Hornblower, Commentary on Thucydides I (1991) on III.50

claims.claim: At Arginusae (406) the generals were tried together, contrary to law; Socrates, among the prytaneis, refused to put the motion; six returned generals, including the younger Pericles, executed; the Athenians later repented.
claims.source: Xenophon, Hellenica I.7; Plato, Apology 32b; Xenophon, Memorabilia I.1.18

claims.claim: The graphe paranomon is first attested c. 415 BC; after 403 laws (nomoi) were separated from decrees (psephismata) and changed by nomothetai.
Madison, Federalist 55: 'Had every Athenian citizen been a Socrates, every Athenian assembly would still have been a mob' (paraphrased in our words).
Melos 416 BC; 'the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must' (V.89, Crawley).
The Thirty killed not fewer than 1,500 Athenians; Critias and Charmides were Plato's relatives; Socrates condemned by about 280 votes to 220 of 501.
claims.source: Athenian Constitution 35.4; Plato, Apology 36a; Diogenes Laertius 2.41

claims.claim: Peisistratus gained a bodyguard by a staged wound (Herodotus 1.59); Dionysius I of Syracuse was voted a bodyguard (Diodorus 13.95).

Modern critics: Bryan Caplan, The Myth of the Rational Voter (2007); Jason Brennan, Against Democracy (2016) (hobbits, hooligans, vulcans; epistocracy, plural voting and epistocratic veto) — summarised in our own words; Levitsky and Ziblatt, How Democracies Die (2018); Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945); Allan Bloom (1987).
Aristotle studied at the Academy 367–347; tutor to Alexander 343; founded the Lyceum 335; was a metic in Athens; 158 constitutions collected; left Athens 323, died 322.

Politics IV.9 (1294b): lot thought democratic, election oligarchic; IV.4 (1292a): demagogues arise where laws are not supreme, the people become a monarch; III.16 (1287a): law as God and reason, man adds the beast; III.1: citizen defined by sharing in judging and office.
Condorcet's jury theorem, Essai (1785); Waldron, 'The Wisdom of the Multitude', Political Theory 23 (1995); Landemore, Democratic Reason (2013).
Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I–II q.105 a.1 reads Deuteronomy 1 and Exodus 18 as a mixed regime of kingship, aristocracy and democracy instituted by God.
Polybius VI on Rome's mixed constitution; Montesquieu, Spirit of the Laws XI.6 (1748).
Acton's 'Power tends to corrupt...' is in a letter to Mandell Creighton, 5 April 1887.
claims.source: Acton, Historical Essays and Studies (1907), appendix

claims.claim: Ambrose refused Theodosius communion until penance after the Thessalonica massacre (390).
claims.source: Ambrose, Letter 51; Theodoret, Church History V.17

claims.claim: Putney Debates 1647; Rainsborough's 'the poorest he that is in England hath a life to live, as the greatest he' (paraphrased).
Liberty Bell cast 1752–53 with Leviticus 25:10 (KJV); Jubilee 2000 debt campaign.
Washington resigned his commission 1783 and declined a third term in 1796.
Chatham collapsed in the House of Lords on 7 April 1778 and died 11 May 1778; Copley's painting 1779.
claims.source: NGA object record; ODNB, Pitt, William

claims.claim: Traditions table: Augustine, City of God IV.4, XIX; Justinian, Novel 6 (535); Calvin, Institutes IV.20.8; John Paul II, Centesimus Annus 46 (1991).
Siedentop (2014), Holland (2019), Habermas (Time of Transitions, 2006) and Pinker (2018) summarised in our own words.
Painting descriptions in 'look' use only the NGA assistive text for each object.
